```{r data-setup, include=FALSE}
# Self-contained load and clean; sets up the core variables used throughout
# this report.
df <- read.csv(
  "data/2019/2019_Food_Access_Research_Atlas_Data/Food Access Research Atlas.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  na.strings = c("NA", "NULL", "")
)

num_vars <- c("Pop2010", "OHU2010", "LA1and10", "HUNVFlag", "Urban",
              "PovertyRate", "MedianFamilyIncome", "TractBlack", "TractKids",
              "TractSeniors", "TractHUNV", "lahunv1share")
for (v in num_vars) df[[v]] <- as.numeric(df[[v]])

core_vars <- c("LA1and10", "PovertyRate", "MedianFamilyIncome", "Urban", "HUNVFlag")
df <- df[complete.cases(df[, core_vars]), ]

# Standardise the two continuous predictors before putting them in an
# interaction model -- keeps odds ratios interpretable as "per 1 SD",
# and puts PovertyRate (0-100) and MedianFamilyIncome (tens of
# thousands) on a comparable scale.
df$PovertyRate_z <- as.numeric(scale(df$PovertyRate))
df$MedianFamilyIncome_z <- as.numeric(scale(df$MedianFamilyIncome))
df$Urban_f <- factor(df$Urban, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("Rural", "Urban"))

# "Plain" composition shares: defined for every tract, not just
# low-access ones, unlike the lah***1share columns -- avoids the
# structural missingness those have (see M2's data-prep notes below
# for where that missingness *is* deliberately used instead).
df$black_share_plain <- df$TractBlack / df$Pop2010
df$kids_share_plain <- df$TractKids / df$Pop2010
df$seniors_share_plain <- df$TractSeniors / df$Pop2010
df$hunv_share_plain <- df$TractHUNV / df$OHU2010
# A handful of tracts have OHU2010 == 0, which would make hunv_share_plain
# Inf/NaN -- flagged rather than dropped, since scale() and randomForest
# can't handle non-finite values. Treat those as missing here instead.
# (106 raw rows have OHU2010 == 0 before the core_vars completeness
# filter above; none remain in the filtered df -- see Data Description.)
df$hunv_share_plain[!is.finite(df$hunv_share_plain)] <- NA
for (v in c("black_share_plain", "kids_share_plain", "seniors_share_plain", "hunv_share_plain")) {
  df[[paste0(v, "_z")]] <- as.numeric(scale(df[[v]]))
}
```

# Executive Summary
<!-- max 1 page. non-technical language, but must include numbers. -->

This report asks whether the relationship between poverty, income and low food access
in US census tracts depends on whether a tract is Urban or Rural. Pooling all tracts
together, poverty rate and income barely separate tracts with low food access from the
rest of the sample (a weak effect). Splitting by Urban/Rural status, however, shows
both relationships pointing in opposite directions in the two area types: in Rural
tracts, low-access areas tend to be poorer and lower-income than other Rural tracts,
matching common intuition, while in Urban tracts, low-access areas tend to be
wealthier and have less poverty than other Urban tracts.

A statistical model that lets poverty and income have different effects in Urban vs.
Rural tracts fits significantly better than a model that assumes one fixed effect
everywhere (p < 0.001). Once poverty and income are modelled together, though, neither
one's own effect literally flips sign by area type. Instead, income is the stronger
signal of low access in Rural tracts, and poverty is the stronger signal in Urban
tracts. Adding a measure of vehicle access to the model did not explain this pattern
(its effect did not shrink the way a true explanation would), and the finding for
poverty was less stable across subsets of the data than the finding for income.

A random forest model, which can detect patterns without the modeller specifying them
in advance, predicted low-access status noticeably better than the statistical model
(71% vs. 66% accuracy), and found that vehicle access and tract demographic makeup
were stronger predictors overall than poverty or income on their own. The main
practical implication: a single poverty or income cut-off is not a reliable way to
flag at-risk areas everywhere. Which measure matters depends on
whether the area is Urban or Rural, and vehicle access deserves more attention as a
screening factor in its own right.

# Background
<!-- 1-2 pages -->

Low-income households are often the ones hit hardest by a long trip to the nearest
grocery store, since the extra time and transport cost falls on people who can least
afford it. That link motivates asking whether poverty and income actually predict low
food access.

The Phase 1 group report (Whithair, Busto, Mehmood and Cai, 2026) looked at access to
large retail food outlets using the Food Access Research Atlas, and found that two
variables often assumed to drive low food access, PovertyRate and MedianFamilyIncome,
barely separated low-access tracts from the rest of the sample once the whole dataset
was pooled together (a weak effect by conventional standards), and taken on its own
this would suggest poverty and income are not strong predictors of low food access at
all.

Splitting the same comparison by Urban/Rural status changes the picture considerably.
Within Rural tracts, low-access areas tend to be poorer and lower-income than other
Rural tracts, which matches common intuition. Within Urban tracts the pattern reverses:
low-access areas tend to have lower poverty and higher income than other Urban tracts.
The group report documented the income-side version of this reversal; checking the
same comparison for poverty rate shows the same pattern holds there too.

A model that lets poverty rate and income have different effects in Urban and Rural
tracts, rather than one fixed slope for the whole country, is the most direct test of
whether this reversal is real rather than noise. That gives two linked, testable
questions for the individual analysis:

**Research question(s).** Does a logistic regression model of low food access status (LA1and10) that includes an
Urban interaction term for both PovertyRate and MedianFamilyIncome fit significantly
better than the same model without the interaction terms? If so, do the Urban-specific
slopes for poverty rate and income actually differ between Urban and Rural tracts in a
way consistent with the reversal seen in the exploratory analysis?

# Data Description
<!-- 1-2 pages -->

The Food Access Research Atlas (FARA) data is a single cross-sectional snapshot from
2019, not a time series: it records one row per US census tract (72,531 tracts across
all 50 states), combining binary low-access flags, tract-level population counts, and
continuous rates/shares describing each tract's demographic makeup and distance to the
nearest large food retailer. Full variable definitions are in the FARA documentation
(USDA ERS, 2019; see References).

This analysis uses a subset of that structure, summarised in \hyperref[tab:varsummary]{Table 1}. **LA1and10**
classifies a tract as low-access at both the 1-mile (Urban) and 10-mile (Rural)
distance thresholds, following the "food desert" measurement approach of Ver Ploeg
et al. (2009). **PovertyRate** is the percentage of the tract
below the poverty line and **MedianFamilyIncome** is the tract's median family income in
US dollars (top-coded at \$250,001); both are standardised before modelling, and **Urban**
(coded 0 for Rural, 1 for Urban tracts) is the interaction variable of interest
throughout. **lahunv1share** is the share of
housing units in a tract with low vehicle access that are also far from a supermarket,
and the four composition shares added in **M3** (Black, children, seniors, and
low-vehicle-access households) are each expressed as a proportion of the tract's own
population or housing units.

```{r data-description-table}
var_summary <- data.frame(
  Variable = c("LA1and10", "PovertyRate", "\\mbox{MedianFamilyIncome}", "Urban",
               "lahunv1share", "Composition shares"),
  Type = c("Binary flag", "Continuous (\\%)", "Continuous \\mbox{(\\$, top-coded)}", "Binary flag",
           "Continuous (share)", "Continuous (share)"),
  `Used in` = c("M0-M3 (response)", "M0-M3", "M0-M3", "M0-M3 (interaction)",
                "M2 only", "M3 only"),
  Missing = c("None", "\\textless1\\%", "\\textless1\\%", "None",
              "27.5\\% (structural)", "1 tract (negligible)"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(var_summary, align = c("l", "l", "l", "l"), escape = FALSE,
      caption = "Variables used in this report: type, role, and completeness\\label{tab:varsummary}")
```

The core variables (**LA1and10**, **PovertyRate**, **MedianFamilyIncome**, **Urban** and
**HUNVFlag**) are close to completely populated: 71,783 of 72,531 tracts (98.97%) have no
missing values on any of them, consistent with the group report's own findings. HUNVFlag
is a raw low-vehicle-access flag used here only to define this complete-case sample, not
as a predictor.
**lahunv1share**'s missingness, by contrast, is structural rather than a data-quality gap: it is
missing for 36% of Urban tracts but under 0.1% of Rural tracts, a pattern tied to area type
rather than an individual data-quality issue, and it is treated that way in the **M2** analysis
below.

One change from the group report's handling of missing data: that report zero-filled
missing demographic tract totals (e.g. **TractBlack**) before computing shares, flagged in
feedback as misleading since a genuinely missing count isn't the same as a genuinely
zero one and treating them alike biases the share downward. The **M3** composition shares
below are instead computed as raw ratios (e.g. **TractBlack** / **Pop2010**), left missing
wherever an input is missing, and excluded case-wise by any model that uses them.

# Ethics, Privacy and Security
<!-- 1-2 pages. Revise the group version in light of any feedback received. -->

This section carries over the Phase 1 group report's Ethics, Privacy and Security
discussion, revised in response to feedback received on that report: the Security
paragraph below now states which measures were actually used, not just which were
possible.

**Ethics.** As in the Phase 1 group report, the clearest ethical risk in this dataset
is that correlations involving demographic composition (e.g. the share of a tract's
population that is Black) could be read as implying those demographics *cause* low
food access, when both are plausibly shaped by the same underlying structural factors
(historical redlining, local zoning, retail investment patterns). This risk is sharper
here than in the group's EDA, because **M3** below fits a random forest that ranks
demographic composition shares by predictive importance, and a ranked importance table
is easy to misread as a causal ranking. Results in this report are presented as
associations useful for predicting which tracts are low-access, not as evidence about
what *causes* low access, and that distinction is kept explicit wherever the random
forest's feature importance is discussed.

**Privacy.** Every variable used is a tract-level count, rate, or flag; there are no
individual- or household-level identifiers anywhere in the dataset, so there is no
realistic risk of re-identifying a specific person. A small number of tracts have very
low population counts and could in principle be distinguishable; none of the analyses
here report results for individual small tracts, only aggregate model coefficients and
bulk tract-level predictions, so this risk does not apply in practice.

**Security.** FARA data is public and needs no additional security measures beyond
normal good practice. These are the actual measures used for this project, not
hypothetical ones: the code and this report are kept in a private GitHub repository
during development, and the only device holding a local copy is password-protected.
With more time, access to that repository could additionally be restricted with
two-factor authentication on the GitHub account, though this was not set up for the
project.

# Exploratory Data Analysis
<!-- 3-4 pages. Subset of the group EDA - only what's relevant to your question. -->

This section shows only the comparisons that motivate the Detailed Analysis, rather
than repeating the group report's full EDA. \hyperref[fig:pooledsplit]{Figure 1} shows PovertyRate (top) and
MedianFamilyIncome (bottom) by LA1and10 status, compared three ways: pooled across all
tracts, then split into Rural and Urban. Pooled, the two groups overlap heavily on
both variables, matching Background's description of a weak pooled effect. Splitting
by Urban/Rural status, however, uncovers the reversal described in Background: within
Rural tracts the pattern matches common intuition, while within Urban tracts it
reverses. This is the entire basis for the research question above: a relationship
that flips sign between two subgroups cannot be captured by a model that only allows
one fixed slope for the whole country, which is exactly what the Urban interaction
terms in **M1** are for.

```{r eda-example, fig.cap="PovertyRate (top) and MedianFamilyIncome (bottom) by LA1and10 status: pooled, then split by Urban/Rural.\\label{fig:pooledsplit}", out.width="90%", fig.align="center", fig.width=8, fig.height=5.5}
df_f <- df %>% mutate(LA1and10_f = factor(LA1and10, labels = c("Not low access", "Low access")))
df_3way <- bind_rows(
  df_f %>% mutate(AreaGroup = "Pooled"),
  df_f %>% mutate(AreaGroup = as.character(Urban_f))
) %>% mutate(AreaGroup = factor(AreaGroup, levels = c("Pooled", "Rural", "Urban")))

p_pov <- ggplot(df_3way, aes(LA1and10_f, PovertyRate, fill = LA1and10_f)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.6, linewidth = 0.4, outlier.size = 0.8, outlier.alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ AreaGroup) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = col_pair) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Poverty rate (%)", fill = NULL) +
  theme_report()

p_inc <- ggplot(df_3way, aes(LA1and10_f, MedianFamilyIncome, fill = LA1and10_f)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.6, linewidth = 0.4, outlier.size = 0.8, outlier.alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ AreaGroup) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = col_pair) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Median family income ($)", fill = NULL) +
  theme_report()

(p_pov / p_inc) + plot_layout(guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

A second relationship worth checking before modelling is between the two predictors
themselves. \hyperref[fig:correlation]{Figure 2} shows PovertyRate and MedianFamilyIncome are moderately
correlated across all 71,783 tracts (r = -0.66): poorer tracts tend to have lower
median income, as expected. This matters later in Detailed Analysis Results, where it
is the reason the two predictors cannot be treated as fully independent effects, and
the reason PovertyRate and MedianFamilyIncome occasionally
point in different directions when the parametric **M1** model is compared against the
non-parametric random forest.

```{r eda-correlation, fig.cap="PovertyRate vs. MedianFamilyIncome across all 71,783 tracts (binned density; r = -0.66).\\label{fig:correlation}", out.width="57%", fig.align="center", fig.width=5.5, fig.height=4}
ggplot(df, aes(PovertyRate, MedianFamilyIncome)) +
  geom_bin2d(bins = 50) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = col_orange, linewidth = 0.6, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#cde2fb", high = "#104281", name = "Tracts") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 260000)) +
  labs(x = "Poverty rate (%)", y = "Median family income ($)") +
  theme_report()
```

A third variable, explored in detail later in **M2**, is lahunv1share: the share of a
tract's housing units with low vehicle access that are also far from a supermarket.
\hyperref[fig:vehicleeda]{Figure 3} shows it by LA1and10 status, split by Urban/Rural, for the tracts where it is
defined (its missingness is structural; see Data Description). In both area types,
low-access tracts have a higher vehicle-access share than other tracts, consistent
with common intuition, but the gap is far larger in Urban tracts (0.07% to 1.51%) than
in Rural tracts (2.57% to 3.27%). That makes vehicle access a plausible candidate to
explain the Urban-dependent poverty/income reversal, a possibility tested formally in
**M2**. **M3** below uses a second, separately-computed vehicle-access measure (hunv_share_plain)
with different missingness, not this one; see its caveats for why the two are not a
straightforward replication of each other.

```{r eda-vehicle-access, fig.cap="lahunv1share (vehicle access share, %) by LA1and10 status, split by Urban/Rural. Y-axis zoomed to the 0-20% range (99th percentile = 19%); whiskers and outliers are computed on the full data.\\label{fig:vehicleeda}", out.width="76%", fig.align="center", fig.width=7, fig.height=3.3}
ggplot(df_f %>% filter(!is.na(lahunv1share)), aes(LA1and10_f, lahunv1share, fill = LA1and10_f)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.6, linewidth = 0.4, outlier.size = 0.8, outlier.alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ Urban_f) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = col_pair) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 20)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Vehicle access share (%)", fill = NULL) +
  theme_report()
```

# Detailed Analysis Results
<!-- 3-4 pages. Must go beyond the EDA - hypothesis test at minimum, ideally a model. -->

## Method

Logistic regression suits this question well: LA1and10 is binary, the
two predictors of interest are continuous, and an interaction term is the right tool
for directly testing whether a slope changes between two groups (Urban/Rural) rather
than eyeballing two separate box plots. Two models are compared: **M0**, with
PovertyRate_z, MedianFamilyIncome_z and Urban_f as main effects only, and **M1**, which
adds an Urban interaction term for both continuous predictors. A formal test comparing
the two models is the test for whether the Urban-dependent reversal seen in the EDA is
real, rather than assuming a single shared slope that happens to look weak overall.

## Data preparation for this analysis

PovertyRate and MedianFamilyIncome are standardised (z-scored) before being used as
predictors, so odds ratios are interpretable as "per one standard deviation" and the
two variables, which are on very different raw scales (0-100 versus tens of thousands
of dollars), are directly comparable within the model. Urban is coded as a two-level
factor (Rural/Urban). The modelling dataset is the same complete-case sample described
in Data Description (71,783 tracts); no imputation is used for **M0**/**M1**. Missingness on
these core variables is small (1.03%) but is concentrated in very small-population
tracts (median Pop2010 1,397 among missing rows vs. 4,027 among complete rows),
consistent with Census suppression of unreliable estimates for small samples; dropping
these tracts has a negligible effect on the modelling sample. **M2** and **M3** use additional variables
with their own missingness patterns, handled separately in those sections.

## Model specification

**M0**: `LA1and10 ~ PovertyRate_z + MedianFamilyIncome_z + Urban_f`

**M1**: `LA1and10 ~ PovertyRate_z * Urban_f + MedianFamilyIncome_z * Urban_f`

Both are fitted by maximum likelihood (binomial family, logit link) on the full
n = 71,783 complete-case sample.

```{r model-fit, include=FALSE}
format_p <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "<0.001", formatC(p, digits = 3, format = "f"))
mcfadden_r2 <- function(m) 1 - (m$deviance / m$null.deviance)

# Shared term labels for every results table in this report, so no table
# shows a raw R variable/interaction name (e.g. "Urban_fUrban:MedianFamilyIncome_z").
term_labels <- c(
  "(Intercept)" = "(Intercept)",
  "PovertyRate_z" = "Poverty rate (z)",
  "MedianFamilyIncome_z" = "Median family income (z)",
  "Urban_f" = "Urban",
  "Urban_fUrban" = "Urban",
  "PovertyRate_z:Urban_fUrban" = "Poverty x Urban",
  "Urban_fUrban:MedianFamilyIncome_z" = "Income x Urban",
  "lahunv1share" = "Vehicle access (lahunv1share)",
  "black_share_plain_z" = "% Black (z)",
  "kids_share_plain_z" = "% Children (z)",
  "seniors_share_plain_z" = "% Seniors (z)",
  "hunv_share_plain_z" = "% Low-vehicle-access (z)"
)

# M0 (baseline): main effects only, no Urban interaction -- the "pooled
# relationship, does Urban matter as its own predictor" model.
m0 <- glm(LA1and10 ~ PovertyRate_z + MedianFamilyIncome_z + Urban_f,
          data = df, family = binomial)

# M1 (interaction): adds the Urban interaction terms -- lets the
# PovertyRate/Income effect flip sign between Urban and Rural.
m1 <- glm(LA1and10 ~ PovertyRate_z * Urban_f + MedianFamilyIncome_z * Urban_f,
          data = df, family = binomial)

# Formal hypothesis test: does adding the interaction terms improve the
# fit significantly? (H0: both interaction coefficients are 0, i.e. the
# Urban/Rural relationship is really the same.)
lrt <- anova(m0, m1, test = "Chisq")
```

```{r vif-check, include=FALSE}
# VIF is checked on M0 (main-effects only) -- it isn't well-defined in
# the usual sense once interaction terms are added, so this checks
# collinearity among the predictors themselves, not the interaction
# structure. Rule used (set in advance): drop MedianFamilyIncome if
# either VIF exceeds 5. Reported inline in prose rather than as its
# own table, since it's a supporting check, not a primary result.
vif_vals <- round(vif(m0), 2)
```

```{r model-results-table, include=FALSE}
m1_table <- tidy(m1, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) %>%
  transmute(
    Term = term_labels[term],
    `Odds Ratio` = round(estimate, 3),
    `Lower CI` = round(conf.low, 3),
    `Upper CI` = round(conf.high, 3),
    `p-value` = format_p(p.value)
  )
```

```{r model-fit-comparison, include=FALSE}
fit_comparison <- data.frame(
  Model = c("M0: main effects only", "M1: with Urban interaction"),
  AIC = round(c(AIC(m0), AIC(m1)), 1),
  `McFadden pseudo-R2` = round(c(mcfadden_r2(m0), mcfadden_r2(m1)), 3),
  check.names = FALSE
)
```

## Results (M0 vs M1)

The formal test comparing **M0** to **M1** is strongly significant (p < 0.001), so the data
reject the null hypothesis that PovertyRate and MedianFamilyIncome have the same
relationship with low food access in Urban and Rural tracts. **M1** also fits the data
better overall (\hyperref[tab:m0vm1]{Table 2}), though the improvement is modest in absolute terms, as
expected for tract-level demographic predictors of a binary outcome.

```{r model-fit-comparison-render}
kable(fit_comparison, align = c("l", "r", "r"),
      caption = "Model comparison: M0 vs M1\\label{tab:m0vm1}")
```

Poverty rate and income are not so closely linked that this becomes a problem
(VIF = `r vif_vals[["PovertyRate_z"]]` for both, consistent with \hyperref[fig:correlation]{Figure 2}'s r = -0.66), so both
were kept in the model. \hyperref[tab:m1or]{Table 3} and \hyperref[fig:m1coef]{Figure 4} break the Urban-specific slopes down by
predictor and area (that slope for each predictor is the main-effect coefficient
*times* the interaction odds ratio, not the interaction coefficient alone):

```{r m1-coef-plot-data, include=FALSE}
# The Urban-specific slope isn't a term glm() reports directly for a
# factor interaction -- it's main effect + interaction. Refitting with
# Urban_f releveled gives that slope (and its CI) directly, rather than
# requiring the reader to add two rows of Table 3 together by hand.
m1_urban_ref <- glm(LA1and10 ~ PovertyRate_z * Urban_f_rev + MedianFamilyIncome_z * Urban_f_rev,
                     data = df %>% mutate(Urban_f_rev = factor(Urban, levels = c(1, 0), labels = c("Urban", "Rural"))),
                     family = binomial)

coef_plot_df <- bind_rows(
  tidy(m1, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) %>%
    filter(term %in% c("PovertyRate_z", "MedianFamilyIncome_z")) %>% mutate(Area = "Rural"),
  tidy(m1_urban_ref, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) %>%
    filter(term %in% c("PovertyRate_z", "MedianFamilyIncome_z")) %>% mutate(Area = "Urban")
) %>%
  mutate(Predictor = ifelse(term == "PovertyRate_z", "Poverty rate", "Median family income"))
```

```{r m1-coef-plot, fig.cap="M1 odds ratios (per 1-SD) by Urban status, with 95% CIs.\\label{fig:m1coef}", out.width="65%", fig.align="center", fig.width=5.5, fig.height=3}
ggplot(coef_plot_df, aes(x = estimate, y = Predictor, xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high, color = Area)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "#898781") +
  geom_pointrange(position = position_dodge(width = 0.4), linewidth = 0.6, size = 0.6) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Rural = col_blue, Urban = col_orange)) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Odds ratio (log scale)", y = NULL, color = NULL) +
  theme_report()
```

```{r model-results-table-render}
kable(m1_table, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
      caption = "M1 (with Urban interaction): odds ratios and 95% CIs\\label{tab:m1or}")
```

Income dominates in Rural tracts and poverty dominates in Urban tracts, with each predictor's weaker
effect nearly nulled out in the other area type -- a more specific finding than the
raw EDA boxplots suggest. Considered one predictor at a time (\hyperref[fig:pooledsplit]{Figure 1}), both poverty
and income appear to flip sign between Urban and Rural, the same reversal already
named in Background. Modelled together, though, neither predictor's own net effect
actually changes sign by Urban status: both stay in the same direction (higher
poverty/income linked to lower odds of low access) in both area types -- only which
predictor dominates changes. Because the two predictors are correlated (\hyperref[fig:correlation]{Figure 2}),
the apparent bivariate reversal for each one considered alone is, at least in part, a
product of shared variance redistributed differently by area type, not two
independent reversals.

## Goodness of fit (chosen model: M1)

```{r goodness-of-fit, include=FALSE}
# Hosmer-Lemeshow: are M1's predicted probabilities well-calibrated,
# not just "better than M0"? LRT/AIC only compare models against each
# other, not whether the chosen model's predictions match reality.
hl_test <- hoslem.test(m1$y, fitted(m1), g = 10)

calib_df <- data.frame(predicted = fitted(m1), observed = m1$y) %>%
  mutate(decile = ntile(predicted, 10)) %>%
  group_by(decile) %>%
  summarise(mean_predicted = mean(predicted), mean_observed = mean(observed), n = n(), .groups = "drop")
```

A formal test of whether **M1**'s predicted probabilities match the data (Hosmer,
Lemeshow and Sturdivant, 2013) rejects good calibration (X-squared =
`r round(unname(hl_test$statistic), 2)`, df = `r unname(hl_test$parameter)`, p < 0.001)
-- expected at this sample size (n ~ 72,000), since the test's power to detect any
deviation, however small, grows with n. The calibration plot (\hyperref[fig:calibration]{Figure 5})
shows most deciles tracking the diagonal closely, but the top decile under-predicts
risk by about ten percentage points (55% predicted vs. 65% observed) -- a gap worth
flagging for the screening use proposed in Conclusions and Recommendations, since it
falls exactly where that use case cares most:

```{r calibration-plot, fig.cap="Calibration plot for \\textbf{M1}: predicted vs. observed low-access rate by decile of predicted probability.\\label{fig:calibration}", out.width="75%", fig.align="center", fig.width=5.5, fig.height=3}
ggplot(calib_df, aes(mean_predicted, mean_observed)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "#898781") +
  geom_line(color = col_blue, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(color = col_blue, size = 2.2) +
  labs(x = "Mean predicted probability (decile)", y = "Observed proportion low-access") +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  theme_report()
```

## M2: does vehicle access explain the reversal?

**M2** checks an optional sensitivity question from the oral assessment: does vehicle
access (lahunv1share, structural missingness; see Data Description) explain the
Urban-dependent reversal? It does not. **M2** adds lahunv1share to **M1** as a plain
main effect, not interacted with Urban, since the question is whether it explains the
existing Urban interaction, not whether it has its own Urban-specific slope.

```{r m2-vehicle-access, include=FALSE}
# lahunv1share has structural missingness (only computed for
# LATracts1==1 tracts) -- refit M1 on the *same* complete-case
# subsample used for M2, so the M1-vs-M2 comparison isn't confounded
# by comparing two different populations.
df_m2 <- df %>% filter(!is.na(lahunv1share))
n_m2 <- nrow(df_m2)
n_full <- nrow(df)

m1_sub <- glm(LA1and10 ~ PovertyRate_z * Urban_f + MedianFamilyIncome_z * Urban_f,
              data = df_m2, family = binomial)
m2 <- glm(LA1and10 ~ PovertyRate_z * Urban_f + MedianFamilyIncome_z * Urban_f + lahunv1share,
          data = df_m2, family = binomial)
```

```{r m2-sample-note, include=FALSE}
pct_m2 <- round(100 * n_m2 / n_full, 1)
```

```{r m2-coefficient-shrinkage, include=FALSE}
# Coefficient-shrinkage comparison: if the Urban interaction
# coefficients move substantially toward 0 once lahunv1share is added,
# that's informal evidence vehicle access explains part of the
# Urban-dependent reversal. If they barely move, the reversal isn't
# mainly a vehicle-access story. Full table rendered in Appendix A.
interaction_terms <- c("PovertyRate_z:Urban_fUrban", "Urban_fUrban:MedianFamilyIncome_z")

shrink_table <- bind_rows(
  tidy(m1_sub) %>% filter(term %in% interaction_terms) %>% mutate(Model = "M1 (refit on M2 subsample)"),
  tidy(m2) %>% filter(term %in% interaction_terms) %>% mutate(Model = "M2 (+ lahunv1share)")
) %>%
  transmute(Model, Term = term_labels[term], Estimate = round(estimate, 3),
            `Std. Error` = round(std.error, 3), `p-value` = format_p(p.value))
```

Restricting to the subsample with vehicle-access data (`r pct_m2`% of the full sample)
already changes the conclusion for poverty: the Poverty x Urban interaction,
significant in the full-sample **M1** (\hyperref[tab:m1or]{Table 3}), is no longer distinguishable from zero
here -- unlike the income-side result, which stays significant under the same
restriction (full estimates in Appendix A, \hyperref[tab:appendixm2]{Table A1}). Adding
lahunv1share itself does not support a simple "vehicle access explains it" story:
both Urban interaction coefficients should shrink toward zero if it did, but instead
income barely moves and poverty grows back to significant -- the opposite.

The more defensible reading: vehicle access correlates with both poverty and the
subsample's composition, making the subsample-only estimate unstable -- not that it
causally explains the reversal. Vehicle access remains worth investigating further
(as Dr McMillan suggested), but this analysis does not show it to be the mechanism
behind either reversal.

## M3: random forest comparison

A second, non-parametric method (random forest, Breiman, 2001) is worth fitting for
two reasons: it can represent any Urban interaction without one being specified in
advance, directly checking whether **M1**'s interaction-term story survives a method
with no fixed functional form; and it satisfies the brief's suggestion to fit an
actual prediction/ML model. It uses the same three predictors as **M1**
(PovertyRate_z, MedianFamilyIncome_z, Urban_f) plus four demographic composition
shares (Black, children, seniors, low-vehicle-access), all seven included directly
since the brief does not call for a feature-selection step.

```{r m3-data-prep, include=FALSE}
mandatory_features <- c("PovertyRate_z", "MedianFamilyIncome_z", "Urban_f")
optional_features <- c("black_share_plain_z", "kids_share_plain_z",
                        "seniors_share_plain_z", "hunv_share_plain_z")
selected_features <- c(mandatory_features, optional_features)

rf_data <- df %>% select(LA1and10, all_of(selected_features)) %>% na.omit()
rf_data$LA1and10 <- factor(rf_data$LA1and10, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("No", "Yes"))
```

The final random forest (300 trees) is trained on a 70% split of the data, stratified
jointly by LA1and10 and Urban status, and evaluated on the remaining 30%.

```{r m3-train-test, include=FALSE}
set.seed(471)

# Stratify the train/test split by LA1and10 (and Urban, since it's
# central to the research question) so both classes and both area
# types are represented proportionally in the test set.
strata <- interaction(rf_data$LA1and10, rf_data$Urban_f)
train_idx <- unlist(lapply(split(seq_len(nrow(rf_data)), strata), function(idx) {
  sample(idx, size = floor(0.7 * length(idx)))
}))
train_df <- rf_data[train_idx, ]
test_df <- rf_data[-train_idx, ]

rf_final <- randomForest(x = train_df[, selected_features, drop = FALSE], y = train_df$LA1and10,
                          ntree = 300, importance = TRUE)
m1_refit <- glm(LA1and10 ~ PovertyRate_z * Urban_f + MedianFamilyIncome_z * Urban_f,
                data = train_df %>% mutate(LA1and10 = as.numeric(LA1and10) - 1), family = binomial)

rf_pred <- predict(rf_final, test_df, type = "prob")[, "Yes"]
m1_pred <- predict(m1_refit, test_df, type = "response")

rf_roc <- roc(response = test_df$LA1and10, predictor = rf_pred, quiet = TRUE)
m1_roc <- roc(response = test_df$LA1and10, predictor = m1_pred, quiet = TRUE)

rf_ci <- ci.auc(rf_roc, method = "bootstrap", boot.n = 500)
m1_ci <- ci.auc(m1_roc, method = "bootstrap", boot.n = 500)

acc <- function(pred, actual, threshold = 0.5) {
  mean((pred > threshold) == (as.numeric(actual) - 1))
}
```

```{r m3-performance-table, include=FALSE}
perf_table <- data.frame(
  Model = c("M1 (logistic)", "M3 (random forest)"),
  `AUC` = round(c(as.numeric(m1_roc$auc), as.numeric(rf_roc$auc)), 3),
  `95% CI` = c(sprintf("(%.3f, %.3f)", m1_ci[1], m1_ci[3]),
               sprintf("(%.3f, %.3f)", rf_ci[1], rf_ci[3])),
  `Test Accuracy` = round(c(acc(m1_pred, test_df$LA1and10), acc(rf_pred, test_df$LA1and10)), 3),
  `Test n` = nrow(test_df),
  check.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r rf-partial-dependence-data, include=FALSE}
# Does the random forest, which was never told about any Urban
# interaction, independently learn an Urban-dependent relationship for
# poverty and income? Partial dependence: vary one feature over a grid,
# fix Urban_f, and average predicted probability over a sample of the
# other features' real joint distribution.
make_pd <- function(model, data, var, grid, urban_level) {
  sapply(grid, function(val) {
    pdata <- data
    pdata[[var]] <- val
    pdata$Urban_f <- factor(urban_level, levels = levels(data$Urban_f))
    mean(predict(model, pdata, type = "prob")[, "Yes"])
  })
}

set.seed(471)
pd_sample <- train_df[sample(nrow(train_df), 5000), ]
pov_grid <- seq(quantile(rf_data$PovertyRate_z, 0.02), quantile(rf_data$PovertyRate_z, 0.98), length.out = 10)
inc_grid <- seq(quantile(rf_data$MedianFamilyIncome_z, 0.02), quantile(rf_data$MedianFamilyIncome_z, 0.98), length.out = 10)

pd_pov <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(x = pov_grid, prob = make_pd(rf_final, pd_sample, "PovertyRate_z", pov_grid, "Rural"), Area = "Rural"),
  data.frame(x = pov_grid, prob = make_pd(rf_final, pd_sample, "PovertyRate_z", pov_grid, "Urban"), Area = "Urban")
)
pd_inc <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(x = inc_grid, prob = make_pd(rf_final, pd_sample, "MedianFamilyIncome_z", inc_grid, "Rural"), Area = "Rural"),
  data.frame(x = inc_grid, prob = make_pd(rf_final, pd_sample, "MedianFamilyIncome_z", inc_grid, "Urban"), Area = "Urban")
)
```

```{r rf-partial-dependence-plot-data2, include=FALSE}
p_pd_pov <- ggplot(pd_pov, aes(x, prob, color = Area, linetype = Area)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Rural = col_blue, Urban = col_orange)) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(Rural = "solid", Urban = "22")) +
  labs(x = "Poverty rate (standardised)", y = "Predicted P(low access)", color = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_report()

p_pd_inc <- ggplot(pd_inc, aes(x, prob, color = Area, linetype = Area)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Rural = col_blue, Urban = col_orange)) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(Rural = "solid", Urban = "22")) +
  labs(x = "Median family income (standardised)", y = NULL, color = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_report()
```

```{r pd-vs-m1-table, include=FALSE}
# Does the forest's own partial-dependence direction (never told about
# any Urban interaction) agree with M1's adjusted Urban-specific slope?
pd_summary <- bind_rows(
  pd_pov %>% group_by(Area) %>% summarise(net_change = prob[10] - prob[1], .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(Predictor = "Poverty rate"),
  pd_inc %>% group_by(Area) %>% summarise(net_change = prob[10] - prob[1], .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(Predictor = "Median family income")
) %>%
  left_join(coef_plot_df %>% select(Predictor, Area, estimate), by = c("Predictor", "Area")) %>%
  transmute(
    Predictor, Area,
    `Forest` = ifelse(net_change > 0, "Rises", "Falls"),
    `M1 OR` = round(estimate, 3),
    `M1` = ifelse(estimate < 1, "Falls", "Rises"),
    Agree = ifelse(Forest == `M1`, "Yes", "No")
  )
```

```{r rf-importance-data, include=FALSE}
importance_df <- as.data.frame(importance(rf_final)) %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("Feature") %>%
  arrange(MeanDecreaseGini) %>%
  mutate(Feature = term_labels[Feature])
importance_df$Feature <- factor(importance_df$Feature, levels = importance_df$Feature)
```

## Results (M3)

**Partial dependence vs. M1.** To check whether the Urban-dependent pattern found in **M1** reflects a real feature of
the data, not an artifact of the regression's parametric form, \hyperref[fig:rfpd]{Figure 6} shows how the
random forest's own predicted probability changes as PovertyRate and MedianFamilyIncome
vary by Urban/Rural status, without the forest ever being told these predictors
interact with Urban status.

```{r rf-partial-dependence-plot, fig.cap="Partial dependence: PovertyRate (left), MedianFamilyIncome (right), by Urban/Rural.\\label{fig:rfpd}", out.width="90%", fig.align="center", fig.width=8, fig.height=3.3}
(p_pd_pov | p_pd_inc) + plot_layout(guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r pd-vs-m1-table-render}
kable(pd_summary, align = c("l", "l", "l", "r", "l", "l"),
      caption = "Random forest's partial-dependence direction vs. M1's adjusted odds ratio, by predictor and area\\label{tab:pdvsm1}")
```

\hyperref[tab:pdvsm1]{Table 4} checks each of the four curves' direction against **M1**'s adjusted odds
ratio. Three of four agree; only Rural poverty does not -- the forest's predicted
probability *rises* with poverty rate there, tracking the raw bivariate relationship
(\hyperref[fig:pooledsplit]{Figure 1}) rather than **M1**'s adjusted Rural coefficient, which is negative net of
income. This disagreement is informative, not a problem: **M1**'s poverty coefficient
holds income fixed, while the forest's curve lets income vary naturally alongside
poverty, the way the two actually move together (\hyperref[fig:correlation]{Figure 2}) -- the two methods
answer different questions, so they need not agree, and for Rural tracts here they do
not.

```{r broader-pattern-data, include=FALSE}
broader_vars <- c("PovertyRate_z" = "Poverty rate",
                   "MedianFamilyIncome_z" = "Median family income",
                   "black_share_plain_z" = "\\% Black",
                   "kids_share_plain_z" = "\\% Children",
                   "seniors_share_plain_z" = "\\% Seniors",
                   "hunv_share_plain_z" = "\\% Low-vehicle-access households")

broader_pattern <- lapply(names(broader_vars), function(v) {
  grid <- seq(quantile(rf_data[[v]], 0.02), quantile(rf_data[[v]], 0.98), length.out = 10)
  pd_rural <- make_pd(rf_final, pd_sample, v, grid, "Rural")
  pd_urban <- make_pd(rf_final, pd_sample, v, grid, "Urban")
  data.frame(
    Predictor = broader_vars[[v]],
    `Rural (net change)` = round(pd_rural[10] - pd_rural[1], 3),
    `Urban (net change)` = round(pd_urban[10] - pd_urban[1], 3),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}) %>% bind_rows() %>%
  mutate(Pattern = ifelse(sign(`Rural (net change)`) != sign(`Urban (net change)`),
                           "Direction differs", "Same direction"))
```

**Broader pattern scan.** A broader scan of the other four **M3** predictors, requested at the oral assessment,
confirms the Urban-dependent pattern is not unique to poverty and income (same
procedure as \hyperref[fig:rfpd]{Figure 6}; full results in Appendix A, \hyperref[tab:appendixbroader]{Table A2}). Three of six show a
genuine Rural/Urban direction flip: PovertyRate (above), % children, and, by far the
largest effect, the share of low-vehicle-access households, where Rural barely moves
but Urban swings sharply -- plausible given dense, walkable Urban tracts combine high
car-free shares with good food access, a link that doesn't hold where Rural distances
are large regardless. The other three (income, % Black, % Seniors) differ in strength
but not direction.

**Predictive performance.** \hyperref[tab:m3perf]{Table 5} shows **M3**'s non-overlapping, higher AUC and accuracy on the same held-out
tracts, making it a meaningfully better predictor than **M1**. This does not contradict
**M1**'s result: **M1** tests a specific hypothesis about how two slopes vary by Urban
status, while **M3** is free to use any combination of features and non-linear
interactions, including ones **M1** never specified.

```{r m3-performance-table-render}
kable(perf_table, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
      caption = "Held-out test performance: M1 vs. M3 (bootstrap 95% CI on AUC)\\label{tab:m3perf}")
```

**Variable importance.** \hyperref[fig:rfimportance]{Figure 7}'s feature importance ranking puts vehicle access (hunv_share_plain_z)
highest and Urban_f lowest of all seven -- not because Urban is unimportant, but
because its contribution in **M1** is entirely through interaction terms that a plain
importance ranking cannot decompose.

```{r rf-importance-render, fig.cap="Random forest variable importance (mean decrease in Gini).\\label{fig:rfimportance}", out.width="57%", fig.align="center", fig.width=5.5, fig.height=3.5}
ggplot(importance_df, aes(Feature, MeanDecreaseGini, fill = MeanDecreaseGini)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#9ec5f4", high = "#184f95", guide = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean decrease in Gini") +
  theme_report()
```

**Caveats.** Two caveats apply to **M1** and **M3** alike, and a third is specific to
comparing **M2** and **M3**. The data are aggregated at the census-tract
level, so any relationship found here is a tract-level (ecological) association that
need not hold for individual households. MedianFamilyIncome is top-coded at
\$250,001, compressing the top of the income distribution and likely understating the
true income effect in the wealthiest tracts. Separately, **M2**'s finding of structural,
non-random missingness in lahunv1share does not apply to **M3**: hunv_share_plain and the
other composition shares are defined for all but a single tract, a negligible gap by
comparison -- a reminder that vehicle access is measured two different ways across **M2**
and **M3** (see EDA), so the two results are not a straightforward replication of each
other.

# Conclusions and Recommendations
<!-- 1-2 pages -->

The Urban interaction in **M1** is real and well-supported (p < 0.001), but the
mechanism is more specific than a simple sign reversal: income dominates the
poverty-income relationship with low food access in Rural tracts, and poverty
dominates it in Urban tracts, rather than either predictor's net effect flipping sign
once the other is controlled for. **M2** finds no evidence that vehicle access explains
this pattern, though the poverty-side finding is less robust to which subset of
tracts is analysed than the income-side finding is. **M3**'s random forest confirms the
interaction model's predictors are useful for prediction (AUC 0.776 vs. 0.686 for **M1**),
while showing that vehicle access and demographic composition shares carry more raw
predictive weight than poverty and income once non-linear interactions are allowed. A
broader scan of the random forest's own predictions confirms Dr McMillan's
oral-assessment suggestion that this isn't unique to poverty and income: three of six
predictors scanned (poverty, % children, and above all vehicle access) show a genuine
Rural/Urban direction flip, with vehicle access the largest reversal found.

**Recommendation.** Tract-level screening should not assume a single poverty or income
threshold works the same way in Urban and Rural areas. Which predictor signals "at
risk of low access" depends on area type, and vehicle access, not just income or
poverty, is worth its own screening variable given its importance in **M3**. **M1**'s
calibration is weakest exactly in the highest-risk decile (Goodness of fit), so any
screening threshold should be validated against observed outcomes rather than applied
directly from the fitted probabilities.

**Limitations.** All three **M3** caveats apply overall (tract-level aggregation, income
top-coding, the two vehicle-access measures across **M2** and **M3**). The analysis is also
observational and cross-sectional (Data Description): none of **M1**, **M2** or **M3** can
distinguish a causal mechanism from a stable correlation, and the Ethics section's
caution about demographic composition shares applies equally here. Future work could
add a variable-importance stability check to **M3**, or revisit **M2** with a wider range of
vehicle-access variables now that **M3** shows vehicle access is the most predictive
feature available.

# Appendix B: Declaration of AI Use {.unnumbered}

Claude Code was used to help check and improve the R code for the statistical and
random forest models, to independently verify numerical claims in the report against
the underlying computations, to act as a sounding board for discussing analysis and
structural decisions, to assist with data visualisation design, and to assist with
Quarto/LaTeX typesetting and English language polishing. All written interpretations
and analytical decisions are my own work.
